title: Wessex Poems and Other Verses
description: Published in 1898, Hardy's first collection of verse after thirty years of novel-writing, with his own illustrations: poems of Wessex landscape, of the dead, of the Napoleonic wars and of the ironies of circumstance.
plot_or_argument: The collection ranges from the ballad-like 'The Dance at the Phoenix' and the Napoleonic 'The Sergeant's Song' to the elegiac 'Friends Beyond' and the sardonic 'Nature's Questioning'.
literary_form: Poetry collection (with the author's own drawings)
historical_context: The 1890s, Hardy's return to the poetry he had written since the 1860s, and the decline of the rural community.
literary_significance: Wessex Poems began Hardy's career as a major poet and set the tone of his verse; it is the volume from which the twentieth-century revival of Hardy's poetry dates.

title: Satires of Circumstance, Lyrics and Reveries
description: Published in November 1914 and the volume that contains the 'Poems of 1912-13', the greatest English sequence of mourning after In Memoriam: the poems written after Hardy's visit to Cornwall and to Emma's birthplace following her death in 1912.
plot_or_argument: The 'Poems of 1912-13' revisit the places of the early marriage — St Juliot, Boscastle, Beeny Cliff, Pendennis — and record the speaker's grief, guilt and belated recognition of the wife he had neglected; the volume also contains the 'Satires of Circumstance' and the lyrics of the Wessex world.
historical_context: The death of Emma Hardy in November 1912, the visit to Cornwall in March 1913, and the Edwardian and Georgian poetry of the period.
literary_significance: The 'Poems of 1912-13' are the central English elegies of the twentieth century; their honesty about a failed marriage made them the model for the modern confessional elegy and established Hardy as a major poet.

title: The Woodlanders
description: Published in 1887 and Hardy's own favourite among his novels: the story of the woodland economy of Little Hintock and of Grace Melbury, educated above her neighbours and returned to marry the woodlander Giles Winterborne.
plot_or_argument: Grace Melbury, the timber merchant's daughter, is educated and returns engaged to Giles Winterborne; she marries the doctor Edred Fitzpiers instead, is betrayed by his affair with Mrs Charmond, and after Giles's death in a storm and Fitzpiers's reform she returns to her husband.
historical_context: The 1880s, the decline of the woodland trades and the coming of the railway, and the position of the educated woman in a rural community.
literary_significance: The Woodlanders is the finest English novel of the woodland economy: its treatment of the destruction of a rural trade by the market and the railway is a key text for the ecological criticism of Victorian fiction.

title: Treasure Island
description: Serialised as The Sea-Cook in Young Folks in 1881-82 and published in 1883: the founding modern adventure novel, and the book that fixed the image of the treasure map, the one-legged pirate and the boy hero for all later fiction.
plot_or_argument: Jim Hawkins finds a treasure map in the sea chest of the dead Billy Bones, sails on the Hispaniola with Squire Trelawney and Dr Livesey, discovers that the crew has been recruited by the mutineer Long John Silver, survives the mutiny and the island, and returns with the treasure.
principal_characters: Jim Hawkins; Long John Silver; Squire Trelawney; Dr Livesey; Captain Smollett; Billy Bones; Ben Gunn; Israel Hands; Blind Pew
literary_form: Adventure novel (serialised as The Sea-Cook in Young Folks, 1881-82)
historical_context: The 1880s, the revival of the romance after the realist dominance of the 1860s-70s, the Stevenson family's lighthouse engineering and the Pacific voyages of the period.
literary_significance: Treasure Island is the origin of the modern adventure novel and of the pirate of popular culture; it established the narrative grammar of the boys' adventure story and made the romance respectable again in English fiction.

title: Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde
description: Published in January 1886 and written in a few weeks after a dream: the story of a London physician who separates the good and evil elements of his nature by a drug, and of the double who takes his place.
plot_or_argument: Mr Utterson, a lawyer, investigates the strange relationship between his friend Dr Henry Jekyll and the violent Edward Hyde; Hyde murders Sir Danvers Carew, Jekyll withdraws, and the final confession explains that Jekyll's potion allowed him to become Hyde at will, until the transformations became involuntary and Hyde took over.
narrative_structure: Three narrators: Utterson's third-person narrative, Lanyon's statement, and Jekyll's full statement of the case.
principal_characters: Henry Jekyll; Edward Hyde; Gabriel John Utterson; Richard Enfield; Dr Hastie Lanyon; Sir Danvers Carew; Mr Poole
historical_context: The 1880s, the new psychology of the divided self, the Darwinian account of the beast within, and the Edinburgh of Deacon Brodie.
literary_significance: Jekyll and Hyde is the central English myth of the divided self: it gave the language the terms for dual personality and addiction, and it stands at the origin of both the modern psychological novel and the horror genre.

title: Kidnapped: Being Memoirs of the Adventures of David Balfour in the Year 1751
description: Published in 1886 and set in the Highlands after the Jacobite rising of 1745: the story of David Balfour, cheated of his inheritance, kidnapped, shipwrecked, and thrown into the company of the Jacobite swordsman Alan Breck Stewart.
plot_or_argument: David Balfour is kidnapped on his uncle's orders, shipwrecked off Mull, joins Alan Breck in the escape from the brig Covenant, is accused of the murder of the Red Fox at Appin, and flees with Alan across the Highlands to Edinburgh, where he recovers his estate.
principal_characters: David Balfour; Alan Breck Stewart; Ebenezer Balfour; Colin Campbell (the Red Fox); James of the Glens; Captain Hoseason; Cluny Macpherson
literary_form: Historical adventure novel (serialised in Young Folks, 1886)
historical_context: The 1750s, the aftermath of Culloden, the Appin murder of 1752, the Highland clearances, and the Scottish legal system.
literary_significance: Kidnapped is the finest English historical adventure novel of the century and the fullest literary account of the Jacobite Highlands; its friendship of David and Alan is one of the great double acts of English fiction.

title: The Master of Ballantrae: A Winter's Tale
description: Published in 1889 and the darkest of Stevenson's romances: the story of the two Durie brothers of the 1745 rising, the one who goes out and the one who stays, and of the hatred that survives across the world.
plot_or_argument: James Durie, the Master of Ballantrae, joins the Jacobites while his brother Henry stays at home and marries the woman they both love; James returns from India and France to torment Henry, and the brothers travel to America, where they die in the North Woods, James's body guarded by Henry until both are found.
principal_characters: James Durie; Henry Durie; Alison Graeme; Ephraim Mackellar; Mr Henry's factor; Secundra Dass; Lord Durrisdeer; Miss Katharine
historical_context: The 1745 rising, the Scottish estates after Culloden, the Atlantic trade and the North American fur trade.
literary_significance: The Master of Ballantrae is Stevenson's most ambitious novel and the finest English treatment of fraternal hatred; its narrators' unreliability and its colonial settings make it a key text for the study of the Scottish novel and empire.

title: A Child's Garden of Verses
description: Published in 1885 and the most influential English children's poetry collection of the century: sixty-four poems of childhood, illness, imagination and the country house, written from the memory of Stevenson's own sickly Edinburgh childhood.
plot_or_argument: The poems move from 'The Land of Counterpane' and the sickroom to the garden, 'The Land of Nod', 'My Shadow', the 'Swing' and 'Foreign Lands', and end with the child's view of the adult world in 'The Unseen Playmate' and 'Happy Thought'.
meter_and_prosody: Mostly four-line stanzas in iambic tetrameter or trimeter, with a few longer lyrical forms.
historical_context: The 1880s, the Victorian invention of childhood as a separate imaginative world, and the Stevenson family's Edinburgh houses.
literary_significance: A Child's Garden of Verses created the modern poetry of childhood: its child's-eye perspective and its unpatronising tone mark the break between Victorian didactic verse for children and the twentieth-century tradition of children's poetry.

title: The Black Arrow: A Tale of the Two Roses
description: Published in 1888 though serialised in 1883: a romance of the Wars of the Roses in which Dick Shelton, a young Lancastrian, takes to the greenwood to avenge his father and win the heiress Joanna Sedley.
plot_or_argument: Dick Shelton escapes from the tutelage of his treacherous guardian Sir Daniel Brackley, joins the outlaw band of the Black Arrow, rescues Joanna Sedley from Sir Daniel, and after the battle of Shoreby and the siege of Tunstall Keep wins her hand.
principal_characters: Richard Shelton; Joanna Sedley; Sir Daniel Brackley; Ellis Duckworth; Bennet Hatch; Lord Shoreby; Clerk of Tunstall
literary_form: Historical adventure novel (serialised in Young Folks, 1883)
historical_context: The 1460s, the Wars of the Roses, and the outlaw tradition of the English ballad and the Robin Hood legend.
literary_significance: The Black Arrow applies the adventure formula of Treasure Island to English history and is one of the earliest and most influential historical novels for boys.

title: The Ebb-Tide: A Trio and Quartette
description: Published in 1894 and the grimmest of Stevenson's Pacific works: three beachcombers in Papeete take command of a plague ship carrying champagne, and the story of what they find on the island they sail to.
plot_or_argument: Herrick, Davis and Huish, destitute in Tahiti, take the schooner Farallone whose crew has died of smallpox and whose cargo is champagne; they reach an island occupied by the missionary Attwater, who holds them in his power, and the novel ends with Huish's death and Herrick's moral awakening.
literary_form: Novel (with Lloyd Osbourne; serialised in To-day, 1893)
historical_context: The 1890s, the Pacific labour trade, the missions, and the Stevenson's own Samoan exile.
literary_significance: The Ebb-Tide is the most direct English fiction of the imperial Pacific and the moral corruption of the beachcomber; it is Stevenson's darkest book and a central text of the literature of colonialism.

title: The Picture of Dorian Gray
description: Published in Lippincott's Monthly Magazine in June 1890 and expanded for book form in 1891: the story of a beautiful young man whose portrait ages and corrupts while he remains untouched, and the central English novel of aestheticism.
plot_or_argument: Lord Henry Wotton persuades Dorian Gray that youth and beauty are the only things worth having; Dorian wishes that the portrait painted by Basil Hallward would age instead of him, and the wish is granted. He lives a life of concealed vice, murders Basil, blackmails Alan Campbell, and finally stabs the portrait, which restores him to his ruined age and kills him.
narrative_structure: Third-person narrative with interpolated chapters of aphorism and a chapter of Dorian's collection of corrupting books.
principal_characters: Dorian Gray; Lord Henry Wotton; Basil Hallward; Sibyl Vane; James Vane; Alan Campbell; Lady Agatha; Lord Fermor
historical_context: The 1890s, the aesthetic movement, the trial of the novel in the press, and the Wilde circle of the Rhymers' Club and the Café Royal.
literary_significance: Dorian Gray is the founding novel of English decadence and the most complete statement of the aesthetic doctrine that life should imitate art; its treatment of concealed desire has made it a central text of queer literary history.

title: The Importance of Being Earnest: A Trivial Comedy for Serious People
description: First performed at the St James's Theatre on 14 February 1895 and the most perfect English comedy of the nineteenth century: the comedy of two young men who both invent a fictitious invalid in order to escape their social duties, and of the women who love them for a name.
plot_or_argument: Algernon Moncrieff invents 'Bunbury', Ernest Worthing invents his invalid brother Ernest; Gwendolen Fairfax and Cecily Cardew both believe they are engaged to a man named Ernest, the engagements collapse on the discovery of the invention, and the play resolves when it appears that Jack was in fact christened Ernest and is Algernon's elder brother.
narrative_structure: Three acts, one set in a London flat and two in a Hertfordshire garden.
principal_characters: John Worthing (Jack); Algernon Moncrieff; Gwendolen Fairfax; Cecily Cardew; Lady Bracknell; Miss Prism; Rev. Canon Chasuble; Lane; Merriman
historical_context: The 1890s, the marriage market, the country-house weekend, and the aesthetic and dandy culture of London.
literary_significance: The Importance of Being Earnest is the greatest English stage comedy since the Restoration and the definitive statement of Wilde's comic method: the epigram as a weapon against Victorian earnestness, and the pun on a name as the engine of a plot.

title: Lady Windermere's Fan: A Play About a Good Woman
description: First performed at the St James's Theatre on 20 February 1892, Wilde's first great social comedy and the play that made his name in the theatre: the story of a young wife's jealousy, a mother's sacrifice and a fan left in the wrong room.
plot_or_argument: Lady Windermere is about to leave her husband for Lord Darlington when Mrs Erlynne, a woman of doubtful reputation, intervenes; Mrs Erlynne is in fact Lady Windermere's mother, who left her husband and child twenty years before, and she sacrifices her own chance of respectability to save her daughter's marriage.
historical_context: The 1890s, the doctrine of the 'woman with a past', the double standard, and the conventions of the well-made play.
literary_significance: Lady Windermere's Fan brought the moral question of the fallen woman onto the fashionable stage in a new key and established the formula of Wilde's social comedy: the society epigram enclosing a serious argument about forgiveness.

title: An Ideal Husband
description: First performed at the Haymarket Theatre on 3 January 1895: the comedy of Sir Robert Chiltern, a rising politician whose career rests on a secret share-dealing of his youth, and of the blackmailer who threatens to expose him.
plot_or_argument: Mrs Cheveley, an adventuress, threatens to reveal that Chiltern sold a cabinet secret to Baron Arnheim; Chiltern's wife Gertrude demands that he resign, Lord Goring engineers the exposure of Mrs Cheveley, and the play ends with Chiltern's career intact and Goring engaged to Mabel Chiltern.
historical_context: The 1890s, the politics of the Commons, financial speculation, and the public morality of the political career.
literary_significance: An Ideal Husband is Wilde's most political play: its subject is the relation between private corruption and public virtue, and its portrait of the blackmailing woman is one of the sharpest in the English theatre.

title: Salomé
description: Written in French in 1891 and published in Paris in 1893 with illustrations by Aubrey Beardsley; the English text appeared in 1894 with a translation by Lord Alfred Douglas. Banned from the London stage by the Lord Chamberlain, it was not performed in England until 1931.
plot_or_argument: Salomé, daughter of Herodias, desires the prophet Jokanaan (John the Baptist), who is imprisoned in Herod's cistern; when he rejects her, she demands his head on a silver charger as the price of dancing the dance of the seven veils, and at the end Herod orders her execution.
literary_form: Tragedy in one act (written in French)
historical_context: The 1890s, the French symbolist theatre, the Decadent movement, and the censorship of the English stage.
literary_significance: Salomé is the central English text of dramatic decadence and the most influential one-act tragedy of the 1890s; its fusion of the biblical, the erotic and the aesthetic made it a scandal and a founding work of the modern theatre of cruelty.
attribution_notes: Written in French; the English version was a translation by Lord Alfred Douglas revised by Wilde.

title: De Profundis
description: Written in Reading Gaol in early 1897 as a letter to Lord Alfred Douglas and published posthumously in 1905 in an abridged form; the complete text appeared in 1962. It is Wilde's confession, his defence and his most sustained work of prose.
plot_or_argument: The letter recounts the intimacy with Douglas, the quarrel and separation, the catastrophe of the trials, and the prison discipline of suffering; it ends with the resolution to accept the past and to return to art.
literary_form: Epistolary essay (letter to Lord Alfred Douglas, written in Reading Gaol)
historical_context: The 1895-97 imprisonment, the prison reform debates, and the aesthetic philosophy under the pressure of disgrace.
literary_significance: De Profundis is the finest English prison narrative since the seventeenth century and the fullest statement of Wilde's late philosophy: that suffering is not to be escaped but understood, and that the artist's subject is his own life.

title: The Ballad of Reading Gaol
description: Published anonymously in 1898 under the prison number 'C.3.3.' and Wilde's last work: a ballad on the execution of Charles Thomas Wooldridge at Reading in 1896, and on the pity and horror of the common criminal's fate.
plot_or_argument: The ballad follows the prison routine, the condemned man's last days, the hanging, and the narrator's meditation on the shared guilt of all men; its refrain 'each man kills the thing he loves' made it one of the most quoted poems in English.
literary_form: Ballad in six parts (published under the pseudonym C.3.3.)
historical_context: The 1890s, the prison system, the campaign against capital punishment, and Wilde's own experience as prisoner C.3.3.
literary_significance: The Ballad of Reading Gaol is the great English poem of prison reform and the last major Victorian poem; its refrain entered the language and its subject made it a founding text of the literature of incarceration.

title: The Happy Prince and Other Tales
description: Published in 1888 and the first of Wilde's two collections of fairy tales: 'The Happy Prince', 'The Nightingale and the Rose', 'The Selfish Giant', 'The Devoted Friend' and 'The Remarkable Rocket'.
plot_or_argument: The swallow helps the gilded statue of the Happy Prince give away its jewels to the poor, and dies with it; the nightingale stains a white rose with its heart's blood for a student who will not be loved; the Selfish Giant is converted by a child, and in the last tale a conceited firework explodes to nothing.
historical_context: The 1880s, the Victorian fairy-tale revival, and the social misery of the 1880s that the tales address.
literary_significance: The Happy Prince is the finest English literary fairy tale of the century and one of the first children's books to make social justice its subject; its fusion of aesthetic beauty and Christian compassion is unique in the period.

title: Intentions
description: Published in 1891 and collecting 'The Decay of Lying', 'Pen, Pencil and Poison', 'The Critic as Artist' and 'The Truth of Masks': the manifesto of English aesthetic criticism.
plot_or_argument: 'The Decay of Lying' argues that life imitates art and that nature is a bad model; 'The Critic as Artist' makes criticism itself an art and the critic a creator; 'Pen, Pencil and Poison' treats the murderer Thomas Griffiths Wainewright as an artist in crime.
literary_form: Collection of critical dialogues and essays
historical_context: The 1890s, the English reception of Pater, Ruskin and the French symbolists, and the periodical culture of the Fortnightly and the Nineteenth Century.
literary_significance: Intentions is the central text of English aesthetic criticism and the most brilliant polemic in Victorian criticism; its paradoxes about art and life shaped the theory of the modern novel and of the criticism of culture.

title: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland
description: Published in 1865 and told first to Alice Liddell and her sisters on a boat at Oxford on 4 July 1862: the founding work of English children's fantasy and the great Victorian book of nonsense.
plot_or_argument: Alice follows a White Rabbit down a hole into a world of talking animals, a Caterpillar with a hookah, a Cheshire Cat, a Mad Tea-Party, the Queen of Hearts and her croquet-ground, and a trial over stolen tarts; she wakes to find herself beside her sister on the bank.
narrative_structure: Twelve chapters, each built on a single encounter or a parodied verse, with Tenniel's illustrations as part of the text.
principal_characters: Alice; the White Rabbit; the Cheshire Cat; the Caterpillar; the Mad Hatter; the March Hare; the Queen of Hearts; the Duchess; the Mock Turtle; the Gryphon
literary_form: Children's fantasy novel (with illustrations by John Tenniel)
historical_context: The 1860s, Oxford and Christ Church, the Victorian fashion for literary nonsense after Lear, and the golden age of the illustrated children's book.
literary_significance: Alice is the founding text of modern children's fantasy and of English literary nonsense: its logic of the absurd, its parody of Victorian didacticism and its refusal to moralise changed what a book for children could be.

title: Through the Looking-Glass, and What Alice Found There
description: Published in 1871 and generally thought the finer of the two Alice books: the mirror-world of chess, with its reversible logic, its chessboard landscape and its great inventions Tweedledum and Tweedledee and the Jabberwock.
plot_or_argument: Alice climbs through the drawing-room mirror into a country laid out as a chessboard and plays her way from pawn to queen; she meets the Red Queen, Tweedledum and Tweedledee, Humpty Dumpty, the White Knight, and wakes as she takes the Red Queen's crown.
principal_characters: Alice; the Red Queen; the White Queen; Humpty Dumpty; Tweedledum; Tweedledee; the White Knight; the Jabberwock; Haigha; Hatta
literary_form: Children's fantasy novel (with illustrations by John Tenniel)
meter_and_prosody: Prose narrative interspersed with parodic verse ('Jabberwocky', 'The Walrus and the Carpenter', 'A-Sitting on a Gate').
historical_context: The 1860s-70s, the game of chess and the algebra of symbols, and the Victorian interest in mirror imagery and reversibility.
literary_significance: Through the Looking-Glass is the most formally perfect children's book in English: its chess structure, its mirror logic and its invented vocabulary ('Jabberwocky', 'chortle', 'galumphing') gave the language new words and the modern literature of the absurd its method.

title: The Hunting of the Snark: An Agony in Eight Fits
description: Published in 1876 and the greatest long nonsense poem in English: the voyage of a Bellman, a Baker, a Butcher, a Barrister, a Billiard-marker, a Banker, a Beaver, a Boots and a Bonnet-maker in search of a creature that may not exist.
plot_or_argument: The crew sails with a map that is a blank, a rule that the Snark may be a Boojum, and the Baker's warning that if the Snark is a Boojum he will 'softly and suddenly vanish away'; the Baker finds the Snark, discovers it is a Boojum, and vanishes.
principal_characters: The Bellman; the Baker; the Butcher; the Barrister; the Banker; the Beaver; the Billiard-marker; the Boots; the Bonnet-maker
meter_and_prosody: Fourteen-line stanzas of anapaestic tetrameter and trimeter with the rhyme-scheme of 'The Lady of Shalott'.
historical_context: The 1870s, the Victorian culture of exploration and classification, and the philosophical debate about the reality of the external world.
literary_significance: The Hunting of the Snark is the most philosophically serious nonsense poem in English: it is at once an allegory of scientific pursuit, of the search for meaning and of the fear of annihilation, and it has never been fully explained, which is its point.

title: Phantasmagoria and Other Poems
description: Published in 1869 and Carroll's first collection of verse, including the title poem 'Phantasmagoria' — a comic dialogue between a ghost and the man he haunts — and 'The Sea-Bathing' and 'A Sea Dirge'.
plot_or_argument: 'Phantasmagoria' stages a conversation between a spectre and an unimpressed householder about the rules of haunting, the etiquette of ghosts and the tedium of the profession; the shorter poems move between parody, sentiment and logical joke.
historical_context: The 1860s, the Victorian vogue for spiritualism and the ghost story, and the Punch tradition of comic verse.
literary_significance: Phantasmagoria is the best comic ghost poem in English and shows Carroll's method at its most characteristic: the application of strict logic to an impossible premise.

title: Sylvie and Bruno
description: Published in 1889 and the strangest of Carroll's books: a double narrative that alternates between the fairy world of Elfland, ruled by the Warden and the Chancellor, and the Victorian country house of the real world.
plot_or_argument: The narrator moves between the fairy kingdom of Sylvie and Bruno and the English world of Lady Muriel and Arthur Forester; the fairy plot turns on the Warden's abdication and the usurping Chancellor, the real plot on a love affair and a death, and the two are linked by the narrator's trances.
literary_form: Fantasy novel (with illustrations by Harry Furniss)
historical_context: The 1880s, Carroll's later interest in logic, spiritualism and social reform, and the Victorian fairy painting of Richard Dadd and Joseph Noel Paton.
literary_significance: Sylvie and Bruno is the most ambitious and least successful of Carroll's fantasies, but it is a key text for the late-Victorian fairy revival and for the study of the double narrative in children's fiction.

title: Dracula
description: Published on 26 May 1897 and the most influential horror novel ever written: the story of the Transylvanian Count who comes to England to found a new empire of the undead, and of the small company that hunts him down.
plot_or_argument: Jonathan Harker visits Count Dracula in Transylvania and escapes; the Count ships to Whitby, where Lucy Westenra is drained and dies, and Mina Harker is bitten; Van Helsing, Seward, Holmwood and Morris pursue the Count back to Transylvania and destroy him at his castle.
narrative_structure: Epistolary collage of journals, letters, telegrams and newspaper cuttings, with Mina's typescript as the organising document.
principal_characters: Count Dracula; Jonathan Harker; Mina Harker; Lucy Westenra; Abraham Van Helsing; John Seward; Arthur Holmwood; Quincey Morris; Renfield
historical_context: The 1890s, the British Empire and the fear of reverse colonisation, the new science of blood transfusion and hypnosis, and the literary vampire from Polidori to Le Fanu.
literary_significance: Dracula is the founding modern vampire novel and one of the most analysed texts in English literature: its treatment of empire, gender, sexuality and science made it the central text of Gothic studies in the twentieth century.
